title: `-0.0` equals `0.0` in comparisons, sorts, grouping and joins
verdict: one zero for equality and order; which zero a group or `unique` keeps depends on `maintain_order`
description: `0.0 == -0.0` is true, `sort` treats them as equal (with `maintain_order` the input order stays), and `group_by`, `unique` and joins put them together. Without `maintain_order`, the group's key and the surviving row of `unique` carry the zero seen first, which can be `-0.0`; with `group_by(maintain_order=True)` the key was `0.0` in a probe where `-0.0` came first. Polars promises neither. Arithmetic still tells the zeros apart (polars-zero-sign).

On the streaming engine, which zero a group key or `unique` keeps varies from run to run: over 300 runs of `[-0.0] + [0.0] * 99_999`, `group_by('x')` kept `0.0` 5 times and `-0.0` 295 times, `unique()` kept `0.0` 13 times; `group_by('x', maintain_order=True)` kept `0.0` every time. sverify does not see it: its written plan reads doubles as the one zero (`polars_engine.conform`), gives `canon` to every operation that can make `-0.0`, and groups on the canonical key (`aggregate`, `distinct`), so every zero it groups is `0.0` (`test_double_group_keys_have_one_zero_and_one_nan`).
No upstream test pins which zero a group key or `unique` keeps, or zero grouping on the streaming engine; it may change between versions.
reference: `ONE_ZERO` (#89): `-0.0` is `0.0` everywhere, so a group key is never `-0.0`.

provenance.notes: `sverify_dev.probe_polars` runs each expression on edge cases (0, ±1, ±2, 3, ±7, the bounds of the integer width; 0.5, ±2.5, 7, 1e308, ±inf, NaN; NULL), one row at a time, and compares each row with Lean's outcome of the Substrait call under each candidate option (`substrait-check --outcomes`). Observations are Polars programs whose result is recorded as it is. Polars 2.1.0 (Python), Rust crates at tag py-2.1.0 (commit 7f902bd3), on macOS arm64.

evidence.note: The same section at tag py-2.1.0.

provenance.notes: Polars's user guide says it generally follows IEEE 754 for `Float32` and `Float64`, with two exceptions: any NaN equals any other NaN and is greater than every non-NaN value, and operations guarantee nothing about the sign of zero or NaN or a NaN's payload (a sort or group by may make every zero +0 and every NaN a positive NaN). It promises no error bound unless a function says otherwise. The user guide is not versioned; the section reads the same at tag py-2.1.0. Comparisons are not among the exceptions, so `-0.0 == 0.0` holds in `Float32` as IEEE 754 compares them, and a sort or group by may make every zero +0, which puts them together. Settles `cmp`'s `Float32` row at docs level. The docs do not promise which zero a group key carries.

evidence.note: `impl_float_eq_ord!` for pf16, f32, f64: NaN equals NaN and is the largest value.
`impl_float_total_ord_kernel!` for f32 and f64: the column comparison kernels.
`canonical_f32` and `canonical_f64`: `x + 0.0`, every NaN one quiet NaN, for hashing (group by, unique, joins).

notes: Equality, order, sorting and hashing of floats are one generic implementation for `f32` and `f64` (and `pf16`), so `Float32` behaves as the `Float64` probes show.
Read at tag py-2.1.0 (commit 7f902bd3). The streaming engine evaluates expressions through polars-expr on each morsel (crates/polars-stream/src/expression.rs), so these kernels serve both engines.

evidence.note: `test_total_ordering_float_series` (slow): every pair of 0.0, -0.0, ±1.0, ±NaN, ±inf, NULL as `Float32` against `Float32` and `Float64` against `Float32`, column against column and against a broadcast first value or literal; `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `eq_missing`, `ne_missing` must follow `reference_ordering_propagating`: NaN equals NaN (also -NaN), NaN is above every number including inf, 0.0 equals -0.0, NULL propagates. Eager `DataFrame.select`, in memory
`test_is_in_float`, `Float32` and `Float64`: NaN `is_in([-0.0, -NaN])` and 0.0 `is_in([-0.0, -NaN])` are both true (eager)
`test_float`, `Float32` and `Float64`: `index_of(-NaN)` finds NaN and `index_of(-0.0)` finds 0.0, on the series, its ascending and descending sorts and a chunked copy (eager and lazy `collect()`)

`test_sort_direct_key_dtypes` with the `f32` key (517 rows with NaN, ±inf, -0.0, NULL), ascending and descending, `maintain_order=True`: the streaming sort must equal the in-memory sort exactly, with the in-memory and the partitioned (`POLARS_SORT_PARTITION_THRESHOLD_BYTES=1`, morsels of 7) sort modes

notes: Pins `0.0 == -0.0` (and neither `<` nor `>`) for `Float32`, in comparisons, `is_in` and `index_of`; the streaming sort of a key with both zeros equals the in-memory one with `maintain_order=True`.

Polars's CI runs the unit tests by default, where a lazy `collect()` without `engine` runs the streaming engine (also once with `POLARS_IDEAL_MORSEL_SIZE=4`), and again with `POLARS_ENGINE_AFFINITY=in-memory` (.github/workflows/test-python.yml#L55-L78, #L168-L178); eager `Series` and `DataFrame` calls run in memory. Read at tag py-2.1.0 (commit 7f902bd3), not run.
Streaming gives what in memory gives on every probe and observation cited here.

s-zero-key-first groups and dedups 100 000 zeros, `-0.0` first, lazily on each engine: `group_by` without `maintain_order`, `unique()` and `unique(maintain_order=True)` keep `-0.0`, the zero seen first; `group_by(maintain_order=True)` gives the key `0.0`, on both engines. That is not the zero seen first, which the description says; reported for review, description unchanged.

`python -m sverify_dev.probe_polars --diff --write` runs each probe one row at a time and on a 6000-row column with `collect(engine='in-memory')` and `collect(engine='streaming')`, and each observation twice: its `df(...)` frame's `select`, `with_columns`, `filter`, `sort`, `unique`, `join` and `group_by` go through the streaming engine the second time (`StreamingFrame`); the `s-` observations collect a lazy query on each engine themselves. Polars 2.1.0 (Python), macOS arm64.

join-nan-zero-null's recorded differ 1 is a tie order: `sort('y')` ties the rows 0.0 and -0.0 (both y = 2), and the engines list them in different orders. The join results are the same set of rows on both engines; it is no engine difference.

Corrects the verdict and description after s-zero-key-first, on both engines: `group_by` without `maintain_order` and `unique` (with and without `maintain_order`) keep `-0.0`, the zero seen first, but `group_by(maintain_order=True)` gives the key `0.0`. The description had said the key is always the zero seen first.

evidence.note: `test_group_by_float`: -0.0 and 0.0 land in one group (and -nan with nan), keys x and (x, a), maintain_order True and False, eager, in memory.
`test_unique`, `test_unique_counts`: [-0.0, -nan, 0.0, None, 1.0, nan] has 4 unique values, counts [2, 2, 1, 1]; the expected 0.0 does not pin the sign (assert_series_equal holds -0.0 == 0.0).
`test_joins`: -0.0 joins 0.0, NaN joins NaN, eager. No upstream test pins which zero a group key or unique row keeps, nor zero grouping on the streaming engine.

evidence.sql: f = pl.LazyFrame({'x': [-0.0] + [0.0] * 99_999}); [math.copysign(1, f.group_by('x', maintain_order=m).agg(pl.len()).collect(engine='streaming').rows()[0][0]) for _ in range(300)], likewise f.unique()
evidence.observed: maintain_order=False: 0.0 five times, -0.0 295 times; maintain_order=True: 0.0 300 times; unique(): 0.0 13 times, -0.0 287 times

evidence.note: Recorded with -0.0 for maintain_order=False; a rerun on 2026-11-08 gave 0.0.
The written plan's group key is 0.0 where Polars alone keeps -0.0.

provenance.notes: Polars 2.1.0 (Python) on macOS arm64, 10 cores, default thread pool. The written plan uses `group_by(..., maintain_order=True)` and `unique(..., maintain_order=True)` on `_float_key` columns, so the varying zero never reaches a result.
